ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: Your back is the part of your body behind you.
explanation: Your back goes from your neck down to your hips. You cannot see your own back without a mirror.
example_sentence: Papa rubs my back when I am sleepy.
real_world_usage: Please help me put my school bag on my back.
collocations: lie on your back; pat on the back; my back
spelling_guidance: Back ends in 'ck'. The c and k work together to make one 'k' sound.
learning_objective: Children can name and point to their back as a part of the body.
illustration_brief: A smiling child seen from behind, wearing a school bag on their back, with a parent gently patting the child's back.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: A field is a big open piece of land with grass or crops.
explanation: Children play games in a field. Farmers grow food like rice in a field.
example_sentence: We play cricket in the field after school.
real_world_usage: Look at the green rice field from the train!
collocations: green field; rice field; playing field
spelling_guidance: In field, 'i' comes before 'e': f-i-e-l-d.
learning_objective: Children can describe a field as a big open area of grass or crops.
illustration_brief: A wide green field with children playing cricket on one side and a farm with rice crops in the distance under a blue sky.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: The floor is the part of a room you walk on.
explanation: Every room has a floor under your feet. We sweep the floor to keep it clean.
example_sentence: We made a rangoli on the floor for Diwali.
real_world_usage: Please do not leave toys on the floor.
collocations: sweep the floor; on the floor; clean floor
spelling_guidance: Floor has a double 'o', but it sounds like 'or'.
learning_objective: Children can name the floor as the surface of a room and use it in everyday sentences.
illustration_brief: A family sitting together on a clean home floor making a colourful rangoli near the doorway, with small diyas around it.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: The ground is the land under your feet.
explanation: The ground is what you stand and walk on outside. It can be made of soil, grass or stones.
example_sentence: Leaves fell on the wet ground in the monsoon.
real_world_usage: Let us sit on the ground and eat our tiffin.
collocations: on the ground; wet ground; sit on the ground
spelling_guidance: The 'ou' in ground says 'ow', like in cow.
learning_objective: Children can use ground to talk about the land they stand on outdoors.
illustration_brief: Children in raincoats standing on wet brown ground with green leaves and small puddles after monsoon rain.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: A lake is a big area of water with land all around it.
explanation: A lake is bigger than a pond. Ducks and fish can live in a lake.
example_sentence: We saw ducks swimming in the lake on Sunday.
real_world_usage: Let us go for a boat ride on the lake with Mama.
collocations: big lake; by the lake; lake water
spelling_guidance: The 'e' at the end is silent and makes the 'a' say its name: lake.
learning_objective: Children can describe a lake as a big body of water with land around it.
illustration_brief: A calm blue lake surrounded by green trees and hills, with ducks swimming and a family standing safely on the path by the lake.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: A parent is a mother or a father.
explanation: A parent loves and looks after a child. Some children have one parent and some have two.
example_sentence: Every parent came to watch our school dance.
real_world_usage: My parents will come to my school sports day.
collocations: parent-teacher meeting; a proud parent; both parents
spelling_guidance: Parent has 'ar' in the middle and 'ent' at the end: par-ent.
learning_objective: Children can explain that a parent is a mother or father who cares for a child.
illustration_brief: A school hall with different families clapping for children dancing on stage: a mother alone, a father alone, and two parents together.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: A plant is a living thing that grows in soil.
explanation: A plant has roots, a stem and leaves. It needs water and sunlight to grow.
example_sentence: I water the plant at home every morning.
real_world_usage: Look, my plant has a new green leaf!
collocations: water the plant; green plant; potted plant
spelling_guidance: Plant starts with 'pl' and ends with 'nt': pl-a-nt.
learning_objective: Children can say that a plant is a living thing and name what it needs to grow.
illustration_brief: A child gently watering a green plant in a clay pot on a sunny balcony.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: A present is a gift you give to someone.
explanation: We give a present to show we care. It is often wrapped in bright paper.
example_sentence: Nani gave me a present on my birthday.
real_world_usage: I made a card as a present for my teacher.
collocations: birthday present; give a present; wrap a present
spelling_guidance: The 's' in present sounds like 'z': pres-ent.
learning_objective: Children can use the word present to talk about giving and getting gifts.
illustration_brief: A happy child giving a box wrapped in colourful paper with a ribbon to a grandparent at a home birthday celebration with balloons.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: A square is a shape with four sides that are all the same length.
explanation: A square has four straight sides and four corners. All the sides are the same size.
example_sentence: I drew a red square in my drawing book.
real_world_usage: Look, this tile on the floor is a square!
collocations: draw a square; a big square; red square
spelling_guidance: In square, the letter 'q' is followed by 'u': squ-are.
learning_objective: Children can recognise and name a square and say that its four sides are equal.
illustration_brief: A large red square on a page with its four equal sides gently marked, beside everyday square things like a floor tile and a cracker biscuit.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: The top is the highest part of something.
explanation: The top is the part that is up high. It is the opposite of the bottom.
example_sentence: The cat sat on the top of the cupboard.
real_world_usage: I put the last block on the top of my tower!
collocations: on top of; at the top; top of the hill
learning_objective: Children can use top to describe the highest part of an object.
illustration_brief: A child placing a final colourful block on the top of a block tower, with an arrow-free soft glow around the highest block.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: A town is a place with homes, shops and roads where people live.
explanation: A town is bigger than a village but smaller than a city. It has schools, shops and parks.
example_sentence: We went to the town to buy new shoes.
real_world_usage: My Nani lives in a small town near the hills.
collocations: small town; in town; busy town
spelling_guidance: Town has 'ow', like in cow and how.
learning_objective: Children can say what a town is and name things they see in a town.
illustration_brief: A cheerful small Indian town with a few houses, a fruit shop, a school, a temple-free neutral clock tower, autorickshaws and people walking on a sunny day.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: A grown-up is a big person, not a child.
explanation: A grown-up has done all their growing. Mums, dads, aunties, uncles and teachers are grown-ups.
example_sentence: At school, I ask a grown-up to help me open my tiffin box.
real_world_usage: I hold a grown-up's hand when we cross the road.
collocations: ask a grown-up; with a grown-up; a kind grown-up
spelling_guidance: Put a short line, called a hyphen, between 'grown' and 'up': grown-up.
learning_objective: Children can say that a grown-up is an adult and know to ask a grown-up for help.
illustration_brief: A smiling teacher in a bright classroom helping a small child open a tiffin box at lunchtime, with other children eating nearby.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: Your shoulder is where your arm joins your body.
explanation: You have two shoulders, one on each side of your neck. You can lift them up and down.
example_sentence: My bag strap sits on my shoulder.
real_world_usage: Let us sing head, shoulders, knees and toes!
collocations: on my shoulder; shoulder bag; tap on the shoulder
spelling_guidance: The 'ou' in shoulder says 'oh': shoul-der.
learning_objective: Children can name and point to their shoulders.
illustration_brief: A smiling child touching both shoulders while singing an action song with classmates in a bright classroom.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: A station is a place where trains stop so people can get on and off.
explanation: At the station, we wait on the platform. The train stops and we climb in.
example_sentence: We went to the station to meet Dadi.
real_world_usage: The train is coming! Let us stand back at the station.
collocations: railway station; at the station; train station
spelling_guidance: The 'tion' at the end says 'shun': sta-tion.
learning_objective: Children can say what a railway station is and what happens there.
illustration_brief: A busy Indian railway station with a train at the platform, a family holding hands standing safely behind the yellow line, and a big clock above.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: The weekend is Saturday and Sunday.
explanation: It comes at the end of the week. Many of us rest and play then.
example_sentence: At the weekend, I play cricket with Papa.
real_world_usage: This weekend we will visit my cousins at their home.
collocations: this weekend; at the weekend; long weekend
spelling_guidance: Weekend is two small words joined: week + end.
learning_objective: Children can say which days make the weekend and talk about what they do at the weekend.
illustration_brief: A simple calendar page with the last two day boxes in a bright colour, next to a happy family playing cricket together in a sunny park.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: A band is a group of people who play music together.
explanation: In a band, each person plays an instrument or sings. Together they make music.
example_sentence: A band played drums and trumpets at my cousin's wedding.
real_world_usage: Our school band will play on Independence Day.
collocations: school band; brass band; play in a band
learning_objective: Children will understand that a band is a group of people making music together.
illustration_brief: A cheerful school band of children in uniform playing drums, a trumpet and a flute on a stage.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: A bat is a wooden stick used to hit the ball in cricket.
explanation: In cricket, you hold the bat with both hands. You swing it to hit the ball.
example_sentence: Ravi held his bat and hit the ball far.
real_world_usage: Can I use your bat when we play cricket after school?
collocations: cricket bat; hold the bat; swing the bat
learning_objective: Children will name a cricket bat and say what it is used for.
illustration_brief: A child in a park holding a wooden cricket bat, ready to hit a ball, with stumps behind them.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: A kitten is a young cat.
explanation: A kitten is a baby cat. It is small and loves to play.
example_sentence: A little kitten slept on our windowsill during the monsoon rain.
real_world_usage: The kitten is chasing a ball of wool!
collocations: little kitten; soft kitten; play with a kitten
spelling_guidance: Kitten has a double t in the middle: k-i-t-t-e-n.
learning_objective: Children will name a kitten as a young cat.
illustration_brief: A small grey kitten playing with a ball of wool on a mat at home.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: A nurse is a person who looks after people who are sick or hurt.
explanation: A nurse works in a hospital or clinic. A nurse gives medicine, puts on bandages and helps people feel better.
example_sentence: The kind nurse put a bandage on my knee at the clinic.
real_world_usage: When I was sick, a nurse at the clinic gave me medicine.
word_family: nurses (plural); nursing (the job of a nurse)
collocations: kind nurse; hospital nurse; clinic nurse
spelling_guidance: The letters ur make the sound in fur, and nurse ends with a silent e.
related_words: doctor; hospital; clinic; patient; medicine; bandage
learning_objective: Children will name a nurse as a helper who cares for sick or hurt people.
illustration_brief: A smiling nurse in a clinic gently putting a bandage on a child's knee while a parent sits nearby.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: A panda is a large black-and-white bear that eats bamboo.
explanation: A giant panda has black patches around its eyes and on its ears and legs. It lives in mountain forests in China and eats mostly bamboo.
example_sentence: My little brother has a soft toy panda on his bed.
real_world_usage: Look at the panda eating bamboo in this book!
collocations: giant panda; baby panda; panda cub
learning_objective: Children will name a panda and describe it as a black-and-white bear that eats bamboo.
illustration_brief: A giant panda sitting in a green bamboo forest, happily chewing a bamboo stick.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: A party is a happy time when friends or family meet to celebrate.
explanation: At a party, people come together to have fun. They may eat, play games, sing and dance.
example_sentence: We had a birthday party at home with cake and balloons.
real_world_usage: Will you come to my birthday party on Sunday?
collocations: birthday party; have a party; go to a party
spelling_guidance: For more than one, change y to ies: parties.
learning_objective: Children will use party to talk about celebrating with friends or family.
illustration_brief: A group of children and family members around a table with a cake, balloons and paper decorations at home.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: A puppy is a young dog.
explanation: A puppy is a baby dog. It grows up to become a dog.
example_sentence: The little puppy wagged its tail when I came home from school.
real_world_usage: Look, the puppy is playing with a ball!
collocations: cute puppy; little puppy; play with a puppy
spelling_guidance: Puppy has a double p in the middle. For more than one, change y to ies: puppies.
learning_objective: Children will name a puppy as a young dog.
illustration_brief: A small brown puppy wagging its tail in front of a house gate, with a child in school uniform smiling.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: Soup is a liquid food made by cooking vegetables or other foods in water.
explanation: We eat soup from a bowl with a spoon. Hot soup feels nice on a cold or rainy day.
example_sentence: On a rainy monsoon evening, Amma made hot tomato soup for all of us.
real_world_usage: Can I have some more soup, please?
collocations: hot soup; tomato soup; a bowl of soup
spelling_guidance: In soup, the letters ou make an oo sound, as in you and group.
learning_objective: Children will name soup as a liquid food that is often eaten warm from a bowl with a spoon.
illustration_brief: A steaming bowl of red tomato soup with a spoon on a kitchen table, with rain falling outside the window.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: Awake means not sleeping.
explanation: When you are awake, your eyes are open and you can see and hear. In the morning, you wake up and then you are awake.
example_sentence: My baby sister was awake early and smiled at me.
real_world_usage: I was still awake when Papa came home.
collocations: wide awake; stay awake; lie awake
spelling_guidance: Awake is a + wake. The e at the end makes the a in wake say its name.
learning_objective: Children will use awake to describe someone who is not sleeping and know its opposite, asleep.
illustration_brief: A smiling child sitting up in bed in the morning with eyes wide open, sunlight coming through the window.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: A cage is a box or room with bars that keeps an animal or bird inside.
explanation: A cage has bars with gaps between them. The animal inside can see out, but it cannot get out.
example_sentence: The parrot at the zoo sat in a big cage.
real_world_usage: The bird cage at the zoo has a swing inside.
collocations: bird cage; in a cage; open the cage
spelling_guidance: The e at the end makes the a say its name, and the g before e sounds like j: c-a-g-e.
learning_objective: Children will understand that a cage is a place with bars where animals or birds are kept.
illustration_brief: A green parrot sitting on a swing inside a large, clean cage with a little water bowl, at a zoo.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: To sail means to travel across water in a boat that has sails.
explanation: A boat can sail when the wind pushes its big cloth sails. The boat moves across the water.
example_sentence: In the holidays, we watched the boats sail across the sea.
real_world_usage: I want to sail on a boat with my family one day.
word_family: sails; sailed; sailing; sailor; sailing boat
collocations: sail across; sail a boat; set sail
spelling_guidance: The letters ai make the long a sound. Do not mix it up with sale, which is about selling things.
learning_objective: Children will use sail to talk about a boat moving across water with the help of the wind.
illustration_brief: A small boat with a white sail moving across calm blue sea, with a family wearing life jackets on board.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: A scarf is a long piece of cloth that you wear around your neck.
explanation: People wear a scarf to keep their neck warm in cold weather. A scarf can be made of wool or cloth.
example_sentence: In winter, Dadi knitted a warm red scarf for me.
real_world_usage: It is cold today, so I will wear my scarf.
collocations: woolly scarf; warm scarf; wear a scarf
spelling_guidance: Scarf ends in f, but for more than one we often write scarves: change f to v and add es.
learning_objective: Children will name a scarf and say that it is worn around the neck to keep warm.
illustration_brief: A child on a chilly winter morning wearing a red woolly scarf around the neck and a matching cap.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: A second is a very short amount of time; there are 60 seconds in one minute.
explanation: A second is very quick. You can clap your hands once in about one second.
example_sentence: The thin hand on the clock moves every second.
real_world_usage: Wait a second, I am tying my shoelace!
collocations: one second; a few seconds; in seconds
spelling_guidance: The c in second sounds like k, and the word ends with -ond.
learning_objective: Children will know that a second is a very short unit of time and that 60 seconds make a minute.
illustration_brief: A big round wall clock with the thin seconds hand moving, and a child clapping once beside it.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: Your stomach is the part inside your body where food goes after you swallow it.
explanation: When you eat, food goes down to your stomach. Your stomach helps to break the food down so your body can use it.
example_sentence: After eating my tiffin, my stomach felt full.
real_world_usage: My stomach is making noises because I am hungry.
collocations: full stomach; empty stomach; stomach ache
spelling_guidance: The ch in stomach sounds like k: s-t-o-m-a-c-h.
learning_objective: Children will name the stomach and say that it is where food goes after eating.
illustration_brief: A simple, friendly diagram of a child's body showing food going down to the stomach, drawn in a soft cartoon style.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: A whale is a very big animal that lives in the sea and breathes air.
explanation: A whale lives in the sea, but it is not a fish. It comes up to the top of the water to breathe air through a hole on its head.
example_sentence: We saw a picture of a blue whale in our science book.
real_world_usage: The blue whale is the biggest animal in the world!
collocations: blue whale; giant whale; baby whale
spelling_guidance: Whale starts with wh. The e at the end makes the a say its name.
learning_objective: Children will name a whale as a very large sea animal that breathes air.
illustration_brief: A big blue whale swimming near the top of the sea and spraying water from the hole on its head.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: An artist is a person who makes art, such as paintings, drawings or clay models.
explanation: An artist uses paint, pencils, clay or other things to make pictures and shapes. Some artists paint walls, and some make pots or rangoli.
example_sentence: The artist painted big, bright peacocks on our school wall.
real_world_usage: When I grow up, I want to be an artist and paint the monsoon rain.
collocations: famous artist; young artist; local artist
spelling_guidance: Think of it as 'art' + 'ist'. The ending '-ist' means a person who does something, like in 'dentist' and 'scientist'.
related_words: painter; painting; brush; sketch; colours; clay
learning_objective: Learners will use the word 'artist' to talk about a person who makes paintings, drawings or other art.
illustration_brief: A cheerful artist on a small ladder painting bright peacocks, trees and a rainbow on a school wall, while a few smiling children watch and hold paint pots and brushes.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: A camera is a machine that takes photos or videos.
explanation: You point a camera at something and press a button. It keeps the picture so you can look at it again later.
example_sentence: Papa used his camera to take photos of our rangoli at Diwali.
real_world_usage: Can I use the camera to take a photo of the sunset?
collocations: digital camera; video camera; point the camera
spelling_guidance: Say it in three parts: cam-er-a. The middle part is spelt 'er', and the word ends with the letter 'a'.
related_words: photo; lens; video; picture; album; photographer
learning_objective: Learners will name a camera and say what it is used for.
illustration_brief: A father holding a camera and taking a photo of a bright, colourful rangoli at a doorstep with glowing diyas, while two smiling children stand proudly beside it.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: A captain is the leader of a sports team.
explanation: The captain helps the team plan, cheers everyone on and makes decisions during a match. In cricket, the captain decides who will bowl.
example_sentence: Riya was chosen as captain of our school cricket team.
real_world_usage: As captain, I told my team to keep trying until the last ball.
collocations: team captain; vice-captain; choose a captain
spelling_guidance: It ends in -ain, not -an: cap-tain.
learning_objective: Learners will understand that a captain leads a team and use the word when talking about sports.
illustration_brief: A girl in a cricket uniform with a captain's armband, standing in a huddle with her teammates on a school ground, everyone smiling and ready to play.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: Cash is money in the form of coins and notes.
explanation: When you pay with coins and notes instead of a card or phone, you are paying in cash. Shopkeepers keep cash in a box or drawer.
example_sentence: Dadi paid cash for the vegetables at the market.
real_world_usage: I counted the cash in my piggy bank before the festival.
collocations: pay in cash; cash counter; some cash
learning_objective: Learners will understand that cash means coins and notes and use it when talking about paying for things.
illustration_brief: A grandmother at a colourful vegetable stall handing coins and notes to a smiling vendor, with a child holding a cloth shopping bag beside her.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: Closed means not open.
explanation: When a shop is closed, you cannot go in or buy anything. A closed door is shut, so you cannot walk through it.
example_sentence: The stationery shop was closed on Sunday, so I bought my notebook on Monday.
real_world_usage: The library is closed today because it is a holiday.
collocations: closed on Sundays; closed for the holidays; the door is closed
spelling_guidance: Just add -d to 'close' to make 'closed'.
learning_objective: Learners will use 'closed' to describe shops and doors that are not open.
illustration_brief: A small neighbourhood shop with its shutter pulled down and a child with a parent standing outside, looking a little disappointed.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: Evening is the time of day between afternoon and night.
explanation: The evening begins when the sun starts to go down. It is a good time to play outside, finish homework or have tea with family.
example_sentence: Every evening, we play cricket in the park after finishing our homework.
real_world_usage: Good evening, Uncle! Are you coming for tea?
collocations: in the evening; this evening; good evening
spelling_guidance: Say it in two beats, eve-ning, and do not add an extra e in the middle.
learning_objective: Learners will identify the evening as a time of day and use it in phrases like 'in the evening'.
illustration_brief: Children playing cricket in a neighbourhood park as an orange and pink sunset fills the sky, with streetlights just starting to glow.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: If clothes fit you, they are the right size for you.
explanation: When your shoes or clothes are not too big and not too small, they fit you. As children grow, old clothes may stop fitting.
example_sentence: My old school shoes do not fit me any more, so Amma bought me a new pair.
real_world_usage: This kurta fits me perfectly for the Diwali party.
collocations: fit well; fit perfectly; does not fit
related_words: size; tight; loose; try on; clothes
learning_objective: Learners will use 'fit' to describe whether clothes or shoes are the right size.
illustration_brief: A child in a clothes shop trying on a new school sweater in front of a mirror, smiling because it is just the right size, with a parent nearby.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: A guitar is a musical instrument with strings that you play with your fingers.
explanation: You pluck or strum the strings of a guitar to make music. It has a long neck and a hollow wooden body.
example_sentence: My cousin played the guitar while we all sang at Dadi's birthday.
real_world_usage: I am learning to play the guitar during my summer holidays.
collocations: play the guitar; guitar lesson; strum the guitar
spelling_guidance: The u after g is silent: g-u-i-t-a-r.
learning_objective: Learners will name the guitar as a string instrument and use the phrase 'play the guitar'.
illustration_brief: A teenager strumming a wooden guitar in a living room while the family sings and claps around a birthday cake for a smiling grandmother.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: If you are sick, you feel ill.
explanation: When you are sick, you might have a fever, a cough or a tummy ache. Resting and seeing a doctor can help you get better.
example_sentence: Arjun fell sick after playing in the monsoon rain, so he stayed home from school.
real_world_usage: I feel sick today, so I will rest and drink warm water.
collocations: feel sick; fall sick; sick leave
spelling_guidance: After a short vowel sound, 'k' is often spelt 'ck', as in sick.
learning_objective: Learners will use 'sick' to describe feeling ill and talk about how to get better.
illustration_brief: A child resting in bed under a blanket with a thermometer, while a caring family member brings a cup of warm soup; rain falling gently outside the window.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: Equipment is the tools and things you need to do a particular activity.
explanation: Bats, balls and helmets are cricket equipment. Microscopes and test tubes are science equipment.
example_sentence: Our PE teacher keeps all the sports equipment in the store room.
real_world_usage: Please help me carry the science equipment to the lab.
collocations: sports equipment; science equipment; a piece of equipment
spelling_guidance: The 'qu' makes a 'kw' sound. Never add -s: say 'pieces of equipment'.
learning_objective: Learners will use 'equipment' as an uncountable noun for the tools needed for an activity.
illustration_brief: A tidy school sports room with shelves of cricket bats, footballs, skipping ropes and cones, and two children happily carrying some out.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: An interview is a meeting where one person asks questions and another person answers them.
explanation: People have interviews to find out about someone's life or work. The answers can be printed in a school magazine or a newspaper.
example_sentence: For our school magazine, we had an interview with our librarian.
real_world_usage: I took notes during my interview with my grandmother about her school days.
collocations: have an interview; give an interview; interview questions
spelling_guidance: Split it into two parts: inter + view. In 'view', the letter 'i' comes before 'e'.
learning_objective: Learners will explain what an interview is and plan a few simple questions for one.
illustration_brief: Two children holding a notebook and pencil, asking questions to a smiling school librarian sitting near bookshelves.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: An invention is something new that someone has made or designed for the first time.
explanation: An invention solves a problem or makes life easier. The wheel and the light bulb are famous inventions.
example_sentence: Ravi's invention for the science project was a tiffin box that keeps food warm.
real_world_usage: My invention is a pencil holder that never falls over.
collocations: a new invention; a useful invention; a great invention
spelling_guidance: It ends in -tion, which sounds like 'shun'.
learning_objective: Learners will explain what an invention is and describe a simple invention of their own.
illustration_brief: A boy proudly showing a homemade tiffin box with a cosy cover at a school science fair, a glowing light bulb drawn above his head as an idea symbol.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: A professor is a teacher at a university or college.
explanation: A professor knows a lot about one subject and teaches older students. Professors also do research to find out new things.
example_sentence: My aunt is a professor who teaches chemistry at a college in Pune.
real_world_usage: A professor came to our school to talk about the stars and planets.
collocations: college professor; science professor; university professor
spelling_guidance: One f and double s: pro-fes-sor. It ends in -or, not -er.
learning_objective: Learners will understand that a professor teaches at a university or college and use the word in context.
illustration_brief: A friendly professor standing in a lecture hall, pointing to a simple diagram on a board while young adult students take notes.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: A scientist is a person who studies the world by asking questions and doing experiments.
explanation: Scientists watch carefully, test their ideas and record what they find. Some study plants, some study space and some study the human body.
example_sentence: At the science fair, Meera dressed up as a scientist and showed her plant experiment.
real_world_usage: I want to be a scientist and find out why the sky is blue.
collocations: young scientist; space scientist; scientists discover
spelling_guidance: It starts with 'sc', and the c is silent: sci-en-tist.
learning_objective: Learners will describe what a scientist does and use the word in a sentence.
illustration_brief: A girl in a lab coat and safety goggles at a school science fair, showing small potted plants and a chart to curious classmates.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: Technology is the tools, machines and computers that people make using science to solve problems.
explanation: Computers, tablets and smart boards in your classroom are all technology. People use technology to make work easier and to learn new things.
example_sentence: Our school uses technology like smart boards to make lessons more fun.
real_world_usage: We used technology in the computer lab to make a slideshow about animals.
collocations: modern technology; use technology; new technology
spelling_guidance: The 'ch' in technology sounds like 'k': tech-nol-o-gy.
learning_objective: Learners will identify examples of technology in daily school life and use the word correctly.
illustration_brief: A bright classroom with children gathered around a smart board and a computer, a teacher pointing at the screen, everyone looking curious and happy.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: To draw a line through a written word to show it is wrong or not needed.
explanation: If you make a mistake while writing, you can cross out the word with one neat line. Then you write the correct word next to it.
example_sentence: Neatly cross out the wrong answer and write the correct one beside it.
real_world_usage: I crossed out the items on my shopping list after Amma bought them.
word_family: crosses out; crossed out; crossing out
collocations: cross out a word; cross out mistakes; neatly cross out
spelling_guidance: 'Cross' has a double s, and adds -es to make 'crosses'.
learning_objective: Use 'cross out' to describe drawing a line through written words when correcting work.
illustration_brief: A close-up of a child's hand drawing a single neat line through a scribbled word in a notebook, with a pencil and eraser nearby; the writing is shown as wavy lines, not real text.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: To be friendly with someone and have a good relationship.
explanation: If you get along with someone, you like spending time together and you do not fight much. We often say 'get along well with' someone.
example_sentence: My cousin and I get along well when we play cricket together during the holidays.
real_world_usage: I get along with everyone in my project group.
word_family: gets along; got along; getting along
collocations: get along well; get along with; get along together
spelling_guidance: 'Along' has only one l.
learning_objective: Use 'get along (with)' to describe friendly relationships between people.
illustration_brief: Two children laughing together while sharing a cricket bat and ball in a park, with a third child joining them happily.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: To become older and change from a child into an adult.
explanation: Everyone grows up slowly over many years, learning new things as they get older. People also use it to talk about the place where they spent their childhood.
example_sentence: When I grow up, I want to be a scientist like my aunt.
real_world_usage: My grandparents tell me stories about the village where they grew up.
word_family: grows up; grew up; grown up; growing up; grown-up
collocations: grow up in; when I grow up; grow up quickly
spelling_guidance: The past forms are irregular: grow, grew, grown – there is no 'growed'.
learning_objective: Use 'grow up' and its irregular past forms to talk about getting older and childhood.
illustration_brief: A gentle sequence of the same child shown as a baby, a schoolchild and a young adult standing in a row, with a small plant growing taller beside each one.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: To give your finished work to a teacher or another person in charge.
explanation: When you hand in homework or a project, you give it to your teacher so they can check it. It is usually done by a certain time.
example_sentence: Please hand in your science notebooks before the lunch break.
real_world_usage: I need to hand in my art project on Monday.
word_family: hands in; handed in; handing in
collocations: hand in homework; hand in on time; hand in a project
spelling_guidance: Add -ed for the past: hand → handed.
learning_objective: Use 'hand in' to talk about giving schoolwork to a teacher.
illustration_brief: A student placing a neat notebook on a pile of notebooks on a teacher's desk in a bright classroom, while the teacher smiles.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: To put a program or app onto a computer or phone so it can be used.
explanation: When you install an app, it gets added to your device and is ready to open. Always ask a grown-up before you install anything new.
example_sentence: Dad helped me install a maths learning app on the family computer.
real_world_usage: Can you help me install the dictionary app on the tablet?
collocations: install an app; install software; install updates
spelling_guidance: 'Install' ends with a double l.
learning_objective: Use 'install' to describe adding apps or programs to a device, and know its opposite 'uninstall'.
illustration_brief: A parent and child sitting together looking at a phone screen showing a progress bar filling up beside a colourful app icon; no readable text.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: To feel happy and excited about something that is going to happen.
explanation: When you look forward to something, you feel happy and excited while you wait for it to happen. It is often followed by a noun or an -ing word, like 'looking forward to meeting you'.
example_sentence: I look forward to the Diwali holidays every year because my cousins come to stay with us.
real_world_usage: I am really looking forward to our school picnic next week!
word_family: looks forward to; looked forward to; looking forward to
collocations: really look forward to; look forward to seeing; look forward to the holidays
spelling_guidance: 'Forward' ends in -ward, not -word.
learning_objective: Use 'look forward to' correctly to talk about future events that make you happy, followed by a noun or an -ing form.
illustration_brief: A smiling child at a desk marking a date on a wall calendar, with a thought bubble showing a family festival celebration with diyas and sweets.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: Not very hot and not very cold; pleasant.
explanation: Mild weather feels comfortable, so you do not need a heavy sweater or a fan. Many places in India have mild weather in early spring.
example_sentence: In Bengaluru, the weather in February is mild, so we can play outside all afternoon.
real_world_usage: It's such a mild evening, so let's go for a walk in the park.
collocations: mild weather; mild winter; mild climate
spelling_guidance: It ends in -ild, like 'child' and 'wild'.
learning_objective: Use 'mild' to describe comfortable weather that is neither too hot nor too cold.
illustration_brief: Children playing in a green park under a soft blue sky with a gentle sun partly behind light clouds, wearing light clothes and smiling.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: A secret word or set of characters that you type to open an account.
explanation: A password keeps your account safe so that only you can open it. A strong password mixes letters, numbers and symbols, and you should never share it with others.
example_sentence: My sister told me never to share my password with anyone, not even my best friend at school.
real_world_usage: I asked Papa to help me make a strong password for my school learning account.
collocations: strong password; enter a password; forget your password
spelling_guidance: It is two words joined together: pass + word, so keep the double s.
learning_objective: Understand what a password is and why it must be kept private and strong.
illustration_brief: A child typing on a laptop screen showing a row of dots in a login box, with a friendly padlock symbol glowing beside it; no readable text.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: A person who writes poems.
explanation: A poet chooses words carefully to share feelings, ideas and pictures, often using rhythm and rhyme. Poets write about nature, people, festivals and many other things.
example_sentence: On Hindi Diwas, a local poet visited our school and read her poems aloud.
real_world_usage: I want to be a poet and write poems about the monsoon.
collocations: famous poet; young poet; poet laureate
spelling_guidance: Say it in two parts, po-et; the o and e are not joined into one sound.
learning_objective: Understand that a poet is a person who writes poems and connect the word to poem and poetry.
illustration_brief: A poet sitting under a tree with a notebook and pen, looking at rain clouds and blooming flowers, with small musical swirls suggesting rhythm; no text.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: Extra and kept in case it is needed.
explanation: A spare thing is one more than you need right now, so you can use it if something gets lost or broken. For example, a spare key helps if the main key goes missing.
example_sentence: I always keep a spare pencil in my pencil box in case my friend forgets hers.
real_world_usage: Do you have a spare eraser I can borrow?
collocations: spare pencil; spare key; spare tyre
spelling_guidance: It ends in -are, like 'care' and 'share'.
learning_objective: Use 'spare' as an adjective to describe extra items kept in case they are needed.
illustration_brief: An open pencil box with two pencils, one being kindly offered by a child to a classmate at the next desk.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: A series of musical notes that make a song.
explanation: A tune is the part of a song you can hum or whistle, even without the words. Some tunes are so catchy that they stay in your head all day.
example_sentence: My grandfather hums the same happy tune while he waters the plants every morning.
real_world_usage: I can play the tune of our school song on my keyboard.
collocations: hum a tune; catchy tune; play a tune
spelling_guidance: The silent e at the end makes the u say its name: tun → tune.
learning_objective: Understand 'tune' as the musical notes that make a song and use it in phrases like 'hum a tune'.
illustration_brief: A grandfather watering potted plants on a balcony at sunrise, with colourful musical notes floating from his lips as he hums.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: To send a file from your computer or phone to the internet.
explanation: When you upload something, it moves from your device up to a website or online space. Download is the opposite, when files come from the internet to your device.
example_sentence: Our teacher asked us to upload photos of our rangoli to the class website.
real_world_usage: I will upload my homework file after Mummy checks it.
collocations: upload a file; upload photos; upload homework
spelling_guidance: It is up + load joined together; there is no space or hyphen.
learning_objective: Use 'upload' correctly and tell it apart from 'download'.
illustration_brief: A tablet on a desk with a picture of a colourful rangoli floating upwards as an arrow towards a soft cloud shape, showing a file being sent online.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: To make someone believe that something is true.
explanation: When you convince someone, you give good reasons or facts so they agree with you. Being polite and using evidence helps you convince others.
example_sentence: Arjun used facts from his science book to convince his friends that the Moon has no light of its own.
real_world_usage: I convinced my brother that recycling paper really helps save trees.
collocations: convince someone that; fully convinced; hard to convince
spelling_guidance: It ends in -vince with a soft c that sounds like s.
learning_objective: Use 'convince' to describe making someone believe something using reasons or evidence.
illustration_brief: A child pointing to a simple diagram of the Sun shining on the Moon in an open book, while two friends look on with nodding, thoughtful faces; no readable text.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: Able to learn, understand and think well.
explanation: An intelligent person or animal can solve problems and learn new things. Intelligence grows when we stay curious and keep practising.
example_sentence: Our science teacher told us that crows are intelligent birds that can use sticks as tools.
real_world_usage: That was an intelligent idea to use the old bottles for our garden project!
collocations: intelligent animal; intelligent question; highly intelligent
spelling_guidance: Remember the double l in the middle and the -ent ending: intel-li-gent.
learning_objective: Use 'intelligent' to describe people, animals or ideas that show good thinking and learning.
illustration_brief: A crow on a garden wall using a small stick to pull food out of a narrow container, while two children watch with wonder.

ipa_source: CMU Pronouncing Dictionary — US English pronunciation
simple_meaning: A piece of art made by carving or shaping stone, wood, clay or metal.
explanation: A sculpture is art you can walk around and see from all sides, not a flat picture. The artist who makes it is called a sculptor.
example_sentence: On our school trip to the museum, we saw an ancient stone sculpture of a dancer.
real_world_usage: We made a clay sculpture of an elephant in our art class.
collocations: stone sculpture; clay sculpture; make a sculpture
spelling_guidance: The artwork ends in -ture (sculpture), but the artist ends in -or (sculptor).
learning_objective: Recognise a sculpture as a three-dimensional artwork and distinguish 'sculpture' from 'sculptor'.
illustration_brief: Children in a museum gallery looking at a carved stone sculpture of a graceful dancer on a pedestal, with a clay model of an elephant on a nearby table.
